newsitem.title: JAPAN: Foreigners line up to issue more samurai bonds.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners line up to issue more samurai bonds.

text.p: The boom in samurai bonds is heating up, with more overseas fund raisers lining up to issue the bonds to yield-hungry Japanese retail investors during the winter bonus season, analysts and underwriters said on Monday.
Many experts expect the trend to last, while others warn that investors may not be fully aware of risks involved in investing in dual currency samurais.
"Investors are attracted by the high coupon and by the unique characteristic of dual samurais that the interest payment is in yen," said a senior analyst at a bank's research arm.

"Those things are emphasised, but risks such as the danger of currency fluctuations are not publicised widely," the analyst said. Underwriters said the volume of dual currency samurai bond issues in November exceeded 300 billion yen in a single month for the first time.
Issues of samurai bonds so far this year have totalled nearly 3.5 trillion yen, of which dual-currency samurais account for nearly 40 percent.

Given the trend, even smaller securities houses have increased their emphasis on the bonds, especially as commissions from stock transactions have fallen due to a long-lasting slump in the domestic stock market.

"The pace of samurai issuing hasn't gone down. The boom is continuing, particularly given the yen's continuing weakness (against the dollar)," said Masaru Hamazaki, deputy manager at Yamaichi Research Institute.
Japanese investors have been actively shifting their funds into samurais and other types of foreign bonds from low-yielding postal savings and bank deposit accounts.

Big names issuing dual currency samurais recently include International Business Machines Corp and General Motors Acceptance Corp, while underwriters say the governments of Thailand and Argentina are waiting to issue samurai bonds.
But some analysts said they cannot understand why the dual-currency samurai issues are so popular.

"Considering the forex fees the investors have to pay when converting (other currencies) into yen after redemption, the issues are not all that attractive," said the senior analyst at the research arm of a bank.
Recent dual currency samurai issues will be redeemed mainly in U.S. dollars, Australian dollars and New Zealand dollars.

In the Tokyo market, brokerages charge a foreign exchange fee of about one yen for each U.S. dollar an investor sells or buys, while the fee is two yen for an Australian dollar and about four yen for a New Zealand dollar.
Holders of the bonds may have to unload them at a big discount if they decide to sell them before maturity, analysts said, due to their low liquidity.
Analysts also said investors may be ignoring the credit risks involved with the bonds.
In early November, international rating agency Moody's Investors Service said there were default risks for some publicly placed yen-denominated samurai bonds.
Kenneth Pinkes, chief credit officer at Moody's, said: "I think it may not be too long before we see one of those public instruments default."
Pinkes said Moody's was looking for ways to alert investors to the risks involved in investing in speculative-grade samurai issues.
However, other market experts disagreed, saying private investors are well informed about the risks they face and understand the problems of currency fluctuations.
"Personally, I'm not underestimating the quality of investors who invest in foreign bonds," said Masayuki Kichikawa, economist at Nomura Research Institute Ltd.
